title: Beneath Its Brilliant Surface, 'Blade Runner 2099' Lacks a Human Soul
author: Judy Berman
body:
For nearly half a century, the Blade Runner franchise has been on the run from the accusation that its future-noir visual style eclipses the substance of its stories. Critics rhapsodized over the look of Ridley Scott’s 1982 film—a box-office flop that gradually achieved cult-classic status on home video—but judged it to be, as Janet Maslin wrote in the New York Times, “a mess, at least as far as its narrative is concerned.” TIME’s Richard Corliss concluded that “Blade Runner, like its setting, is a beautiful, deadly organism that devours life.” Denis Villeneuve’s 2017 sequel, Blade Runner 2049, fared somewhat better in theaters and with reviewers, though the critiques were of a similar nature. In the years since I took in that 164-minute epic on the biggest screen available, those hazy, saffron-tinted, almost tangibly toxic landscape shots of a bombed-out wasteland that used to be Las Vegas have stayed with me more than the busy plot.

That its mise-en-scène is more memorable than its storytelling may strike Blade Runner’s most devoted audience as a feature, not a bug. When movies attract cult followings, it’s usually the immersive vibe that keeps fans coming back. Television is a different medium, though, one that can be greatly enhanced by technical artistry but needs to be anchored in a compelling narrative and characters with depth in order to hold our attention episode after episode. The speculative worlds of sci-fi TV must be as intricately constructed as they are aesthetically awesome. Prime Video’s Blade Runner 2099, an eight-part limited series that will stream in full on Nov. 25, never quite overcomes its big-screen legacy. Its visual ambition is astounding. Yet that bleak beauty continues to obscure the personalities of its protagonists and the shape of their society.

As its title suggests, 2099 takes place a few generations after 2049. Maybe because the environmental and corporatocratic dystopia of the original Blade Runner’s then-near-future, now-recent-past 2019 Los Angeles was becoming hard to distinguish from our reality, showrunner Silka Luisa (Shining Girls) adds a major dread-enhancing development. Once enslaved to build “Off-world” colonies for refugees of an increasingly uninhabitable Earth, replicants—the flesh-and-blood humanoids engineered by the monolithic Tyrell Corporation to be “more human than human,” i.e., smarter, stronger, and 20 times more productive than us—have overthrown their inferior masters. Now, as they endeavor to restore the global ecosystem, humanity is the underclass relegated to grunt work. Of course, not every human submits. Rebels assume false identities to fight their oppressors. And just as earlier installments followed LAPD officers called blade runners, who are tasked with killing rogue replicants, this one centers around a unit of Los Angeles replicant cops rooting out rogue humans. Confusingly but perhaps necessarily, given the franchise’s branding, they’ve appropriated the blade runner moniker.

Olwen is one such blade runner, now just days away from the preordained death date with which all replicants are born; that this character is played by Michelle Yeoh, who at 64 has lost none of her action-star prowess, is its own implicit argument against planned obsolescence. As she attempts to stay stoic about her demise, she’s partnered with Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human fugitive protecting her disabled younger brother, Elias (Lewis Gribben). Cora's desperate circumstances have driven her to go undercover as a blade runner. It isn’t easy for a human to impersonate a replicant. While the subtle differences in appearance can be faked, replicants aren’t just superior to humans by every quantifiable metric—they also supposedly lack empathy, a side effect of being gestated to adulthood in artificial wombs rather than raised by loving parents.

As tends to be the case in odd-couple, buddy-cop stories, Cora and Olwen have more in common than they know. A draconian spoiler list prevents me from getting too specific about their joint quests, but suffice to say that the human’s rough past has equipped her to blend in with her taciturn new colleagues and the replicant has a greater capacity for interpersonal connection that she realizes. Schafer and Yeoh come from very different onscreen backgrounds (while Yeoh earned global fame as the queen of Hong Kong action movies, Schafer is best known for her arresting work as the artistic love interest of Zendaya’s character in HBO’s lurid and downbeat Euphoria), but both excel at layering vulnerability beneath a stolid mask.

This is not the most creative premise. Even so, it could’ve made an adequate foundation for a show that really engaged viewers—who are still predominantly human, I’m told—with Cora, Olwen, the mostly underwritten characters around them, the relationships among all of the above, and the overlapping societies in which they’re situated. The texture of everyday human life in L.A., such as it is under the boot of the Übermenschen humanity created, doesn’t get much attention. Nor do we understand the larger philosophies or motivations or social structures of the replicants, who can’t reproduce sexually and for whom “ongoing relationships” are proscribed. A peepshow-esque establishment where physically optimized replicants try on prosthetics like pregnant bellies and saggy, elderly skin offers the most telling glimpse at their fantasy lives. These are the details great sci-fi shows like Andor and The Expanse are built on. Here, they’re few and far between. Our understanding is, for the most part, limited to the goals that drive Olwen and Cora and various villains in their hunts for particular objects and people—video-game stuff. (Would it shock you to learn that the owners of this IP do indeed envision video games in its future?) Part of the problem is how little 2099 shows us of the relationships these characters are so invested in. Rather than replicants who are more human than human, we get humans who, in the mootness of their personalities, are more replicant than replicant.

Screen time that might’ve been spent on narrative world-building is instead given over to aesthetic world-building. For all that it lingers on eye candy long enough to induce a sugar coma, the series really does look incredible. Production designers Paul Inglis and Chloe Arbiture, working with huge art and effects teams, have done a spectacular job expanding on Blade Runner’s seedy, cyberpunk cityscapes and the glowing desolation of 2049. There are imposing corporate interiors of classical proportions, massive brutalist complexes reclaimed by nature, abandoned metropolises whose arched, white buildings recall the eerie tableaus of Giorgio de Chirico. Human slums are grubby and cramped but irrepressibly colorful. This is all far easier to do than it was 44 years ago, yet the sheer number of vividly rendered settings and the fact that the series looks so much more real than the typical Marvel VFX job makes it a true technical achievement. If these visuals are destined to be repurposed as backdrops for some big-budget, open-world Blade Runner video game, then 2099 will be a gift to gamers most of all.
